title: A Glasshouse for the Radiators
premise: Sebastian Coldharbour, once the conservatory's celebrated young pianist, returns two decades later as its night janitor, hiding her identity behind a mop and a borrowed surname. At her estranged father's funeral, a stranger named Ilse Varga addresses the family by their pre-emigration name — a name Sebastian was told to forget — and leaves behind a letter containing one untranslatable sentence in their lost mother tongue. As Sebastian deciphers it, she uncovers that her father traded the family's history, and her childhood, for sanctuary, and that Ilse is the daughter of the man he betrayed to do it. The sentence turns out to be her mother's last testimony; translating it means choosing between exposing her father's survival bargain and letting the family's true name die with him. In the end, Sebastian reads the sentence aloud in the glasshouse at dawn — not as accusation or absolution, but as inheritance — and signs her real name beneath it.
about_author: Ulyana Dunmore grew up between a northern port town and her grandmother's kitchen-table stories, which she was told never to write down. She spent ten years restoring historic greenhouses before turning to fiction about people who live inside other people's buildings.

chapters.title: The Tenant of Glass
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. She begins her janitorial shift at the conservatory she once performed in as a prodigy, navigating corridors where staff don't recognize her and she prefers it that way. A small moment — polishing a plaque bearing her childhood name — establishes her double life. Emotional beat: quiet self-erasure mistaken for peace.

chapters.title: A Funeral in the Wrong Language
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. At her father's funeral, relatives perform grief in polished English while Sebastian stands at the edge like hired help. An unfamiliar woman, Ilse Varga, approaches the family and greets them by the old name — the one forbidden since before Sebastian can remember. Emotional beat: the past arriving uninvited, cracking Sebastian's careful anonymity.

chapters.title: What the Letter Said Before It Was Translated
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. Ilse presses an envelope into Sebastian's hands outside the crematorium: a single handwritten sentence in the family's dying language, plus an address and a deadline. Sebastian, half-fluent only, recognizes her mother's handwriting from old recipe cards. Emotional beat: dread braided with hunger — the first thing in years she wants.

chapters.title: Night Shifts and Half-Words
chapters.summary: Alternating Sebastian and Ilse POVs. Sebastian works nights, decoding fragments with a stolen dictionary and memory; Ilse, meanwhile, researches the Coldharbour/Varga entanglement in archives, revealing her own grievance. Their near-encounters build tension. Emotional beat: two women circling the same wound from opposite sides.

chapters.title: The Brother Who Kept the Ledger
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. Ilse confronts Sebastian's older brother Marek, who manages the estate, and learns he has known about the sentence for years — and helped bury it. Flashback reveals the wartime-era bargain: names surrendered, testimony suppressed, safety purchased. Emotional beat: complicity exposed; Marek's shame curdles into threat.

chapters.title: Frost on the Panes
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. Marek discovers Sebastian has the letter and demands she hand it over, invoking the family's fragile respectability and her precarious job. The conservatory's heating fails overnight, and she works by lamplight among dying plants, finishing the translation alone. Emotional beat: isolation hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Sentence, Whole
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. The translation completes itself at 4 a.m.: her mother's testimony naming what her father did to secure the family's passage — including betraying Ilse's father. Sebastian finally understands why the name was buried and why she was made a tenant of her own life. Emotional beat: devastating clarity; grief and fury fused.

chapters.title: Two Daughters of Two Liars
chapters.summary: Ilse and Sebastian share a scene, first-person alternating. In a café neither chose, they lay out their inheritances: Ilse's stolen father, Sebastian's stolen name. They argue, nearly part, then realize the sentence belongs to both of them. Emotional beat: enemies becoming reluctant co-heirs.

chapters.title: Marek's Offer
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. Marek offers Sebastian full ownership of the conservatory and the family fortune if she burns the letter and disappears properly this time. Standing in the restored glasshouse, warm again, she sees exactly what survival costs and who pays. Climactic choice crystallizes. Emotional beat: temptation rendered as a gilded cage.

chapters.title: Read Aloud at Dawn
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV, closing with Ilse present. At sunrise in the glasshouse, before Marek and the scattered family, Sebastian reads her mother's sentence aloud in the old language, then translates it plainly. She refuses the offer, claims her true name, and gives Ilse the original letter. Emotional beat: costly belonging — no longer a tenant, not yet forgiven, but finally an owner of her own story.
